1.pericope_label: Blessed be the Lord my strength, which teacheth my hands to war and my fingers to fight

schools.summary: Augustine keeps the old title and reads it as mystery: David put five stones in his scrip and hurled but one, so that the five Books were chosen and unity conquered, and he cut off the giant’s head with the giant’s own sword, as the devil is overthrown with his own weapons when those he held turn their tongues against him; and where others found mere repetition in hands and fingers he finds a division of operation with a unity still remaining, since the diversities of operations are all worked by one Spirit.

Calvin takes the internal evidence to point past Goliath to the enemies of the kingdom after David came to the throne, notes that some refer the psalm to the war with the Ammonites and Syrians, and refuses the rendering rock on the ground that the explanation added immediately afterwards is of a man formed for war under God’s teaching, so that David though of a warlike spirit was not born for warlike enterprises but needed to undergo a change. Gill takes the first word for the author and giver of natural strength of body, fortitude of mind and spiritual strength alike, and notes that it may be rendered my rock, which three old versions turn into my God.

Spurgeon observes that strength without skill is little gain, since untrained force injures the man who has it and endangers those about him, so that the psalmist blesses God as much for the teaching as for the strength, and he adds that the Lord not only gives strength to his saints but is their strength; he allows the reading rock but objects that it does not consort so well with the teaching of the hands. Henry notes that a prayer for further mercy is fitly begun with a thanksgiving for former mercy, follows the multiplied words of the opening, observes that the deliverer is emphatic in the original as a deliverer always near, and remarks that the man who had sheltered in natural strongholds and lately taken a fortified one depends on none of them, the divine attributes and promises being fortifications far exceeding those of nature or art.

Clarke collects the headings the versions give the psalm, four of them calling it a psalm of David against Goliath and another placing it when David slew Asaph the brother of Goliath, reports Calmet’s guess that it belongs to the period after the death of Absalom, holds it an abridgment of an earlier psalm preserving the same ideas and forms of expression, and divides the two clauses by weapon, the hands for sword and battle-axe and spear and the fingers for the bow and the sling.

Keil and Delitzsch report that the Greek version adds the title against Goliath, on the testimony of an early scholar only in a few copies, and that an Aramaic paraphrast read the evil sword of the tenth verse as the sword of Goliath after a rabbinic source. Ellicott prefers to render the first word rock rather than strength, and gives the second clause more literally as a training of the hands for war and the fingers for fight.

debates: Is the first word strength or rock? Gill allows both and Ellicott prefers rock, while Spurgeon and Calvin object that rock does not consort with the teaching of the hands that follows, Calvin adding that the explanation given immediately afterwards settles it.

Does the psalm belong to the fight with Goliath? Keil and Delitzsch trace the title to the Greek version and an Aramaic paraphrast, Clarke reports both that heading and a guess placing the psalm after the death of Absalom, and Calvin argues from internal evidence for the enemies of the kingdom after David came to the throne.

Are hands and fingers a mere repetition? Augustine denies it and finds in the fingers a division of operation within a unity; Clarke divides them by weapon, the hands for sword and spear and the fingers for bow and sling.
outliers: Augustine reads the five stones in the scrip as the five Books, of which one was hurled, so that unity conquered.
Clarke reports a version that dates the psalm to the slaying of Asaph the brother of Goliath.
Spurgeon argues that untrained force is a danger to its possessor and to those around him, which is why the teaching is blessed as much as the strength.
themes: a warrior who had to be taught

2.pericope_label: My goodness, and my fortress, my high tower and my deliverer: Lord, what is man, that thou takest knowledge of him: man is like to vanity, his days are as a shadow that passeth away: bow thy heavens, O Lord, and come down: rid me and deliver me out of great waters

schools.summary: Spurgeon makes the contrast of the third verse the whole point, since man is too little to be described at all and too feeble and fickle to be the rock of anyone’s confidence, so that the wonder is that God should stoop to know him, a thing more remarkable than if the greatest archangel should study ants or befriend mites; and he presses the picture of the fifth verse, that the heavens are the Lord’s own and he who exalted them can bow them, that the strongest pillars of earth cannot bear the weight of his finger, and that if his touch sets the mountain peaks smoking then all mortal power opposed to him must end in smoke.

Gill calls God not only good but goodness itself, allows the rendering my mercy or my grace, offers the breath of the mouth after one rabbi or a vapour for the vanity of the fourth verse, and allows a literal sense of clouds hanging low and heavy with rain before taking the descent for a manifestation of God, reporting that some read it as a prayer for the incarnation.

Clarke guesses that the subduing clause points to a nation once more reduced to loyal obedience, perhaps after the rebellion of Absalom, and finds a play in the Hebrew of the fourth verse, since the word for vanity is the name of Abel, so that man is like to Abel and exposed to the same miseries and murderers, in millions of cases the hands of brothers being lifted to shed the blood of brothers. Wesley reads the subduing as God disposing the people’s hearts to receive their king, and keeps to the plain sense elsewhere, that the smoking is like that of the mount at the giving of the law, that the strange children are either the heathen nations or rebellious countrymen, and that the vanity spoken is vain brags and threatenings which come to nothing.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the third verse as a variation on an earlier psalm made with other verbs, the word for knowing carrying the sense of loving intimacy and the phrase for the son of man taking an Aramaic form, and remark that the third stanza hangs together with the second even more loosely than the second with the first; they observe that the deeds an earlier psalm celebrates are here turned into petition and that the rescue out of great waters is taken over word for word, yet insist that so great an imitator has much of his own, instancing the verb for sending forth lightning. Ellicott takes the goodness of the second verse for a shortened form of the phrase God of my grace, notes that the verb and number of the subduing clause differ from the parallel psalm and that some manuscripts and two versions carry the other reading, admits that the occasion for the sentiments of the third and fourth verses is not clear, renders the sixth verse literally as lighten lightning with a verb peculiar to this place, derives the sense of the word for rid from cognate languages, and refers the right hand of falsehood to the custom of raising the right hand in an oath.

debates: How much of this psalm is borrowed? Keil and Delitzsch show the rescue out of great waters taken over word for word from an earlier psalm and yet insist the imitator has much of his own; Ellicott agrees that the theophany uses the classic language but points to touches of originality, including a verb peculiar to this place.

Why does the reflection on human frailty stand here? Ellicott admits the occasion is not clear and offers the humility of a warrior, a reflection over the corpses of comrades, or a blending of the two; Keil and Delitzsch note only that the stanza hangs loosely on what precedes.

Whose people are subdued? Ellicott notes the singular here against the plural of the parallel psalm, with manuscripts and versions divided; Clarke reads a nation restored to obedience after a rebellion, and Wesley the hearts of a people disposed to receive their king.
outliers: Clarke finds the name of Abel in the word for vanity, and asks what wars are but fratricide in the great human family.
Spurgeon compares God stooping to know man with an archangel making a study of ants or befriending mites.
Ellicott reports that the verb of the sixth verse occurs nowhere else, and renders it lighten lightning.
themes: goodness itself, or the God of my grace
a psalm that quotes an older psalm
the name of Abel inside a word
a prayer for the heavens to stoop

9.pericope_label: I will sing a new song unto thee, O God: upon a psaltery and an instrument of ten strings will I sing praises unto thee: it is he that giveth salvation unto kings: rid me and deliver me from the hand of strange children

schools.summary: Henry notes that fresh favours call for fresh returns of thanks and that we must praise God for mercies hoped for by promise as well as for those received by providence, and points out that great kings cannot save themselves, having life-guards and armies and every device of safety, while it is God who gives them their salvation and could do it without those means. Spurgeon makes the new song a turning from the false to the true and a fresh channel cut by gratitude, then qualifies the instrument at length: music can do no more than represent praise, the real praise being in the heart, so that when it drowns the voice and artistic skill takes a higher place than hearty singing it is time instruments were banished from public worship, though where they stay subordinate to the song he will not prohibit them or condemn those who use them.

Gill grounds the newness of the song in mercies that are new every morning, adds that it suits a dispensation in which all things are become new and reports one Jewish interpreter referring it to the days of the Messiah, puts the salvation of kings in terms of victory won not by the force of armies or by military skill but by the right hand of the Lord, and notes that the plea for rescue is repeated from earlier in the psalm to show the vehemence and importunity of the request.

Clarke reads the new song as one of peculiar excellence and undertakes to pour forth all his gratitude and skill on the composition; and he takes the tenth verse further than the others by defending the institution of monarchy, which he holds to be in principle from God, the form of government that has principally prevailed in the course of providence and on the whole been most beneficial to mankind, and therefore under God’s peculiar protection.

Ellicott notes that the divine name of the ninth verse is the only instance of it in the last two books of the psalter apart from one psalm that is itself a compilation from two older songs. Keil and Delitzsch take the word joining the tenth verse to what follows in the sense of because, report that the Greek version read a different word and so made the following description a picture of the prosperity of the enemies, and grant that this makes the join close while thinking it improbable that so carefully drawn a description should belong to the enemies; they add that in the verses following we hear a language altogether peculiar.

debates: Whose prosperity is described in the verses that follow? Keil and Delitzsch report a Greek reading that assigns it to the enemies and makes the join closer, but judge it improbable that so carefully drawn a description should be theirs.

What place have instruments in worship? Spurgeon allows them while they stay subordinate to the song and would banish them when artistic skill outranks hearty singing, adding that he greatly prefers to do without; Henry brings in the ten strings because all is little enough for such praise.

What does salvation given to kings mean? Henry makes it the limit of royal power, Gill turns it into victory not won by armies, and Clarke uses it to defend monarchy as the form of government most beneficial to mankind.
outliers: Spurgeon gives the longest treatment of church music in the psalm, ending with a rule for when instruments should be banished and an admission of his own preference.
Ellicott observes that the divine name here is the only one of its kind in the last two books of the psalter, apart from one compiled psalm.
Clarke turns the tenth verse into a defence of monarchy as a divinely protected institution.
themes: music that represents praise but is not praise

12.pericope_label: That our sons may be as plants grown up in their youth, that our daughters may be as corner stones: that our garners may be full: that our oxen may be strong to labour: happy is that people whose God is the Lord

schools.summary: Spurgeon takes the figures for what they teach about a household: the sons matter first to the state, and if they do not grow in their youth, when will they grow, since plants may grow crooked and so may our sons; daughters unite families as corner stones join walls and adorn them as polished stones garnish a building, so that home becomes a palace when the daughters are maids of honour and the sons noble in spirit.

Gill reports from five old versions the reading by which the sons and daughters and barns belong to the wicked and describe the outward happiness of the enemies, notes that supplying the words who say would make the description their vain boasting, but follows the other versions and takes the whole for the petition of a good prince concerned for his people; he keeps to the plainer senses of the fourteenth verse, the oxen burdened with flesh or with young, and counts the temporal blessings of the last verse highly valuable and a matter for thankfulness.

Clarke reads the passage as inventory rather than petition, since the three promised blessings of the fruit of the body, the fruit of the ground and the increase of the cattle were actually in possession, and insists the expressions be understood in the present tense, adding that a people in such a state who then revolted were doubly guilty, ungrateful to God and man alike; he reads the fourteenth verse as a report on public order, with no robbers or house-breakers or marauding parties and no incursions carrying off property and people, his enemies either become friends or held aloof by fear; and he says a people so blessed who rebel must have the curse of God and man. Wesley makes the sons the strength and hopes of a nation, glosses the corner stone as strong and beautiful, and takes the going out either to meet an invader or into captivity.

Ellicott works through the possible renderings of the relative that opens the twelfth verse, rejects each on grammatical grounds and concludes that what follows is a fragment of another poem unconnected with the earlier part of the psalm; he takes the word for plants to denote a young vigorous tree lately planted, prefers a suggested reading of reproductive in their youth, notes that the word for corner stones occurs only once besides and comes from a root meaning to conceal; and he declares the fourteenth verse full of obscurities, rejecting oxen laden with produce or fat or young and proposing instead that the line speaks of princes firmly established, while giving the alternatives for the breaking in, the going out and the complaining, including Ewald’s rendering of no abortion and a Syriac version with none barren among the cattle. He closes by defending the beatitude, since only a narrow and one-sided religion can see anything out of place in a blessing of plenty and peace.

debates: Whose household is described in these verses? Gill reports five old versions reading whose, which assigns the prosperity to the enemies and makes it their vain boast, and allows that supplying who say would give the same result, but follows the other versions and takes it for the psalmist’s petition.
How does the passage connect with what precedes? Ellicott finds the opening relative impossible to construe on any of the usual devices and concludes that what follows is a fragment of another poem.

What are the strong oxen of the fourteenth verse? Ellicott rejects oxen laden with produce, with fat, or with young, and proposes princes firmly established; Ewald keeps the pregnant cattle and renders the next phrase no abortion; Gill and Clarke keep the plain rendering.
outliers: Clarke reads the whole passage as a present inventory of blessings enjoyed rather than a prayer for blessings wanted, and draws from that the guilt of those who then rebelled.
Ellicott calls the fourteenth verse full of obscurities and lists five separate points on which he cannot settle the sense.

Ellicott defends the psalm’s closing beatitude of plenty against those who would spiritualise it away, holding that rejoicing in temporal blessings opens rather than closes the way to the psalms’ spiritual depths.
themes: a fragment joined by an impossible word
sons as saplings, daughters as corner stones
